title: AWS Lambda Pushes Serverless Toward Long-Running Workloads
gist: AWS Lambda now lets functions on Lambda Managed Instances run up to 90 minutes, six times the prior 15-minute cap, blurring the line between a Lambda invocation and a traditional server and drawing praise for agentic-workload use cases alongside community warnings about idempotency risk and cases where durable functions or ECS/Batch remain the better economic fit.

themes.theme: The timeout extension and its history

insights.claim: AWS Lambda now allows functions running on Lambda Managed Instances to run for up to 90 minutes, six times longer than the previous 15-minute limit, while the limit remains unchanged at 15 minutes for traditional synchronous requests.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: A 6x timeout increase for a specific execution mode removes a longstanding architectural constraint for steady-state and long-running serverless workloads without changing the guarantees of the classic event-driven Lambda model.
insights.locator: AWS Lambda now allows functions running on Lambda Managed Instances

insights.claim: Lambda's timeout increased from 5 minutes at its 2014 launch to 15 minutes in 2018, and that 15-minute ceiling became a recurring pain point requiring workarounds for workloads such as media processing, financial calculations, data processing and ETL, AI inference, and web scraping or large file transfers.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Establishes that the 90-minute increase addresses a persistent, named category of customer pain that has existed for roughly eight years since the last timeout change.
insights.locator: Lambda's timeout increased from 5 minutes at launch in 2014

insights.claim: Lambda now offers three execution tiers: standard functions for event-driven workloads with a 15-minute timeout, MicroVMs for user- or AI-generated code that can run up to 8 hours, and Lambda Managed Instances for steady-state workloads that now support up to 90 minutes with multiple requests per instance and access to EC2-based pricing and compute options without infrastructure management.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: AWS is segmenting serverless into distinct execution models tuned to different workload shapes rather than a single one-size-fits-all Lambda, a mental model useful for choosing the right compute tier.
insights.locator: Lambda now offers two main forms

insights.claim: Rajesh Pandey, principal engineer at AWS, said long-running Lambda functions have been one of the most repeatedly requested customer features, and that a lot of the duct-tape workarounds built around Lambda's maximum execution duration can now come off.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Direct AWS confirmation that this was sustained, high-demand customer feedback rather than a speculative feature, suggesting strong immediate adoption is likely.
insights.quote: I've lost count of how many times customers have asked when are you guys going to build, "Long-running Lambda functions." Finally, it's here. A lot of the duct tape built around Lambda’s maximum execution duration can now come off.
insights.locator: Rajesh Pandey, principal engineer at AWS, highlights

insights.claim: Lambda Managed Instances also now support Graviton5-powered EC2 instances, and the extended 90-minute timeout is supported in all regions where Lambda Managed Instances are available.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Pairing the timeout extension with the latest Graviton silicon generation signals AWS is bundling compute-efficiency gains alongside the flexibility increase.
insights.locator: The increased timeout is not the only recent announcement

themes.theme: Blurring the server/serverless line, and its risks

insights.claim: Yan Cui, serverless expert and AWS Hero, said the change further blurs the line between "running a server" and a Lambda invocation, but that it makes sense especially for the "Lambda for agentic workflows" use case.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Explicitly ties this infrastructure change to AI agentic workloads, suggesting cloud providers are reshaping core compute primitives around the longer, less predictable execution patterns that agents require.
insights.quote: Part of me is sad that this further blurs the line between "running a server" and a Lambda invocation. But it does make sense, especially for the "Lambda for agentic workflows" use case.
insights.locator: Yan Cui, serverless expert and AWS Hero, writes

insights.claim: AWS warns that longer-running Lambda functions require extra care with network connections, temporary credentials, and duplicate execution: developers must ensure connections and credentials remain valid for the full runtime, design operations to safely handle retries and duplicate processing, and note that Lambda does not guarantee exactly-once processing, so the window for retries and duplicate deliveries increases with longer runtimes.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Longer execution windows amplify existing at-least-once delivery risk; teams adopting the 90-minute timeout for payments or database writes must proactively build idempotency rather than assume Lambda handles it.
insights.quote: Lambda does not guarantee exactly-once processing. With longer-running functions, the window for retries and duplicate deliveries increases.

insights.claim: AWS recommends using Powertools for AWS Lambda to implement idempotency in function code so operations like payments or database writes produce the same result even if executed more than once.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Points to a specific, concrete tool teams should adopt before relying on the extended timeout for financially or operationally sensitive workloads.
insights.locator: You can use Powertools for AWS Lambda to implement idempotency

insights.claim: Community member Dull_Caterpillar_642 warned that if a job takes 90 minutes there's a good chance it should use durable functions instead, and that unless the code is doing meaningful work the entire time rather than waiting on other systems, Lambda's economics may not work out as favorably as alternatives like ECS Tasks or AWS Batch.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: A direct cost-efficiency caution against defaulting to the new long-running Lambda option: teams should evaluate whether their 90-minute workload is compute-bound (good fit) or wait-bound (better served by durable functions or container-based compute).
insights.quote: If it's taking 90 min, there's a good chance you should be using something like durable functions
